claims.text: Rapid induction melting produces non-equilibrium solid-solution regions in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
Thermal exposure causes the non-equilibrium solid-solution regions to preferentially decompose into stable intermetallic compounds.
The products of decomposition may include Mg-rich phases and Al-rich intermetallics.
Decomposition into intermetallic compounds increases microstructural heterogeneity.
The increased heterogeneity includes additional phase boundaries.
Heterogeneous intermetallic phases create local electrochemical-potential differences.
Local electrochemical-potential differences promote galvanic corrosion.
Phase boundaries created during transformation facilitate oxygen diffusion during high-temperature oxidation.
The thermally transformed alloy will have a higher corrosion rate than the as-cast non-equilibrium baseline.
The thermally transformed alloy will oxidize faster than the as-cast non-equilibrium baseline.
Faster oxidation will be observable as greater mass gain or increased oxide-scale formation.
The proposed initial material is a predominantly solid-solution, non-equilibrium Mg-containing HEA.
The proposed initial material has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Annealing or elevated-temperature exposure at approximately 300–600°C can provide sufficient opportunity for phase transformation.
The prediction does not apply when the alloy remains a homogeneous solid solution after thermal exposure.
The magnitude of the corrosion and oxidation changes depends on alloy composition and thermal-exposure parameters.
The exact phase assemblage after thermal exposure may vary.
